subject: Pathology
summary: Precursor lesions are abnormal cells that may progress to cancer if untreated. Recognising them early guides surveillance and treatment, especially in low‑resource settings where definitive therapy may be limited.

sections.p: Precursor lesions are abnormal epithelial or glandular cells confined to the epithelium, showing atypia but no invasion. Diagnosis relies on histology and grading.
b: CIN: cervical intraepithelial neoplasia; CIS: carcinoma in situ; PIN: prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia

t.b: Atypical cells with nuclear enlargement, hyperchromasia, increased mitoses, but no basement‑membrane breach.
Positive in most CIN, some esophageal and penile lesions.
Strong p16 and Ki‑67 indicate high‑grade dysplasia.

sections.p: Severity is graded by depth of epithelial involvement and cytologic atypia. Staging informs risk of progression and surveillance intervals.
b: CIN 1: mild dysplasia; CIN 2: moderate; CIN 3: severe, high‑grade. PIN 1–3 similarly graded.

sections.p: Infections, chronic irritation, and genetic mutations drive precursor lesions. Tropical infections and environmental exposures are common in low‑resource settings.
b: TB, HIV – immunosuppression increases dysplasia risk.

sections.p: Often asymptomatic; when symptoms occur, they reflect the organ involved.
b: Cervical dysplasia – abnormal Pap smear, post‑coital bleeding.

sections.p: Tests confirm diagnosis, grade severity, and guide management. Availability may be limited; clinical judgment is essential.

t.b: ASC-US, LSIL, HSIL categories guide colposcopy.
High‑grade dysplasia warrants surveillance or resection.

sections.p: Rapid progression, invasion, or associated symptoms require urgent care.
b: Sudden worsening of hematuria, dysphagia, or pain.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden increase in hematuria, dysphagia, or pain; rapid lesion growth; invasive features on imaging.

faq.a: Yes, especially high‑grade lesions if untreated.
Low‑grade lesions may regress; high‑grade usually require treatment.

faq.q: Is HPV vaccination effective for existing lesions?
faq.a: It prevents new infections but does not treat existing dysplasia.

exam: Explain the grading system for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia and its clinical implications.
Describe the management pathway for a patient with high‑grade bladder carcinoma in situ in a low‑resource setting.
Discuss how chronic schistosomiasis can lead to bladder dysplasia and outline prevention strategies.
